questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A breast cancer patient post-chemotherapy developed a low-grade fever with anemia and leukocytopenia (&lt;4000/cm3; DNC: 30). Which of the following antibiotics will not be used in the empirical management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Linezolid cannot be used in this patient as bone marrow suppression is a side effect of this drug and hence it can worsen the post-chemotherapy bone marrow suppression in this patient.

Linezolid can cause myelosuppression which can present as anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and pancytopenia. It is commonly associated with thrombocytopenia and is seen 7-10 days following administration. This is usually reversed on discontinuation of the drug. 

Other adverse effects of linezolid:

  • It inhibits mitochondrial protein synthesis and may lead to peripheral neuropathy, optic neuritis, and lactic acidosis in patients receiving the drug for longer durations.
  • It can cause serotonin syndrome when coadministered with adrenergic or serotonergic drugs like SSRIs due to its nonspecific MAO inhibition.

It is a protein synthesis inhibitor of the class oxazolidinones. It mainly acts against gram-positive organisms. It is approved for the treatment of the following conditions:

  • Skin and skin structure infections by staphylococcus(Both MRSA and MSSA) and streptococcus.
  • Community-acquired pneumonia due to streptococcus pneumoniae.
  • Nosocomial pneumonia due to staphylococcus aureus. 

Other options:

Cefepime: It is a fourth-generation antipseudomonal cephalosporin. It is useful in enterobacter and pseudomonas infections that are resistant to other cephalosporins.

Piperacillin-Tazobactam- It is a combination of piperacillin which is a ureidopenicillin and tazobactam which is a beta-lactamase inhibitor. It is useful in various infections including nosocomial infections, intraabdominal infections, pneumonia, and UTI. It is highly effective against E Coli and Klebsiella.

Meropenem: It belongs to the carbapenem group of beta-lactam antibiotics. They are more active against gram-negative organisms. Coadministration of cilastatin is not required with this drug. (Cilastation should be coadministered with imipenem as imipenem is sensitive to renal peptidase degradation)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: CIostridium difficile associated diarrhea occurs maximally due to:
questions.explanation:
Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea is mostly due to lincosamides such as clindamycin

Antibiotic-associated colitis is caused by Clostridium difficile infection due to the destruction of the normal gut microbial flora by the use of antibiotics. The antibiotics most frequently implicated include clindamycin, fluoroquinolones and broad-spectrum penicillins, and cephalosporins

Clostridium difficile infection occurs frequently in hospitals and nursing homes where antimicrobial use is high and the environment is contaminated by C. difficile spores.

Although all antibiotics can cause the condition, the most commonly implicated are:

  • Clindamycin
  • Third-generation cephalosporins (cefotaxime, ceftriaxone, cefuroxime, and ceftazidime) 
  • Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, and moxifloxacin)
  • Broad-spectrum penicillins

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A 53 year old man is found to have stage 2 hypertension without any co morbidities. Which drug will you start?
questions.explanation:
Chlorthalidone is one of the first choice drugs in the treatment of hypertension without any comorbidities.
 
First-choice drugs used in the treatment of hypertension in patients without any comorbidities include:
  • Thiazide diuretics: Chlorthalidone is usually preferred to hydrochlorothiazide.
  • Calcium channel blockers: Extended-release, long-acting dihydropyridines are preferred.
  • ACE inhibitors: Captopril is preferred for the initiation of therapy. Enalapril and ramipril twice daily may also be used.
In the presence of any associated conditions or comorbidities, the first choice drugs for the treatment of hypertension would be as follows:
 
Conditions associated with hypertension
First choice drugs for hypertension
Diabetes
Chronic kidney disease with proteinuria
Inhibitors of renin-angiotensin system.
Angina
Beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers
Heart failure
ACE inhibitors and alpha+beta blockers such as carvedilol
Benign prostatic hyperplasia
α1 Blockers
Pregnancy
Labetalol
Atrial fibrillation
Diltiazem and verapamil

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A patient presents to the emergency department with diarrhea, sweating, excessive lacrimation, and salivation. His pulse rate is 55/min and his plasma cholinesterase level was 50U/mL. Which of the following can be used to treat this patient?
questions.explanation:
The clinical features are suggestive of organophosphate poisoning and IV atropine is the treatment of choice.

The organophosphates commonly used as pesticides are anticholinesterases. Toxicity occurs by excessive inhalation of vapors, ingestion, or percutaneous absorption. It inhibits the cholinesterase activity which results in an increase of acetylcholine, leading to cholinergic symptoms.

The predominant initial signs are of muscarinic excess which includes: (DUMBBELSS)

  • Diarrhea
  • Urination
  • Miosis
  • Bronchospasm
  • Bradycardia
  • Emesis
  • Lacrimation
  • Salivation
  • Sweating

This may be followed by cognitive disturbances, convulsions, and neuromuscular blockade.

Treatment:

  • Maintenance of vital signs particularly respiration
  • Removal of clothing and washing of the skin
  • IV atropine 2- 5 mg. If IV administration is not possible, then 2 mg IM every 5-10 minutes (till muscarinic symptoms disappear)
  • Pralidoxime, a cholinesterase reactivator can also be used for treatment

Pegloticase is used in the treatment of chronic gout.

Pegloticase is a pegylated uricase (urate oxidase). It catalyzes the enzymatic oxidation of uric acid into allantoin, which is a more soluble and inactive metabolite.

It is used in the treatment of severe, refractory chronic gout or in cases where other urate-lowering therapies are contraindicated.

Angiotensin 1 receptor acts via Ca2+ channels. It does not act through second messengers via the K+ channel.

questions.question: What dose of epinephrine is used in anaphylactic shock?
questions.explanation:
Epinephrine (1:1000 solution) 0.5 ml via intramuscular route is preferred in the treatment of anaphylactic shock.

For intravenous use, 1:1000 adrenaline must be further diluted to 1:10,000 and should be used very cautiously as slow bolus.

There is a much greater risk of causing harmful side effects by either inappropriate dosage or misdiagnosis of anaphylaxis when using IV adrenaline. Hence, IM injection is preferred over intravenous (IV) bolus because it is faster in many situations and safer (lower risk of cardiovascular complications, such as severe hypertension and ventricular arrhythmias).

For intramuscular, subcutaneous, and inhalational (nebulization) routes of administration, 1:1000 dilution can be used. 

In cardiac arrest, the 1:1000 adrenaline must be diluted to 1:10,000 for IV use. The recommended dose of epinephrine is 1mg = 10 mL of 1:10,000 solution IV administered every 3 to 5 minutes during resuscitation as per the CPR guidelines.

Epinephrine is also used in the treatment of hypotension, to induce local vasoconstriction to reduce the diffusion of local anaesthetics and to induce bronchodilation in asthma and COPD.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: 9. What is the function of phase I reactions in xenobiotics?
options: To make the compund more permeable across the membranes
To extract functional proteins through oxidation and reduction reactions
To directly conjugate the compound and facilitate excretion
To introduce functional groups for further metabolism
questions.correct_answer: To introduce functional groups for further metabolism
questions.explanation:
The function of phase I reactions in xenobiotic metabolism by CYP enzymes is to introduce functional groups for further metabolism. Drugs are chemical substances foreign to the body called xenobiotics. Metabolism of xenobiotics is needed to render nonpolar, lipid-soluble compounds to polar, water-soluble, and lipid-insoluble ones so that they are excreted in the renal tubules without being reabsorbed. The elimination of drugs has been divided into 2 phases: * Phase 1 reactions: which include oxidation, reduction, or hydrolytic reaction. The phase 1 enzymes lead to the introduction of functional groups such as –OH, –COOH, –SH, –O–, or NH2. The addition of functional groups does little to increase the water solubility of the drug but can dramatically alter the biological properties of the drug. Reactions carried out by phase 1 enzymes usually lead to the inactivation of a drug.  * Phase 2 reactions, in which enzymes catalyze the conjugation of the substrate (the phase 1 product) with a second molecule. Phase 2 enzymes facilitate the elimination of the drug by producing a metabolite with improved water solubility that facilitates drug elimination from the tissue, normally via efflux transporter. Pearl PM1734: Phases of drug metabolism Phase I reactions: They attach functional groups to the drugs. This usually leads to the inactivation of the drug.  Examples: * Oxidation * Reduction * Hydrolysis * Cyclisation * Deamination Phase II reactions: They attach conjugates to the drugs. This facilitates drug elimination from the tissue.  Examples: * Glucuronide conjugation * Sulfate conjugation * Glycine conjugation * Glutathione conjugation * Acetylation * Methylation All phase II reactions are mainly conducted by the non-microsomal enzymes except glucuronidation.

2. Reverse Tolerance B. Repeated use of a drug in one category confers tolerance to other drugs in the same category
3. Cross Tolerance C. Increase in response with repetition of the same dose of the drug
questions.explanation:
The correctly matched option is 1A, 2C, 3B.  * Acute tolerance refers to rapid tolerance developing with repeated use on a single occasion, such as in a “binge.” For example, repeated doses of cocaine over several hours produce a decrease in response to subsequent doses of cocaine during the binge. This is the opposite of sensitization, observed with an intermittent-dosing schedule. * Reverse tolerance or sensitization refers to an increase in response with repetition of the same dose of the drug. Sensitization, in contrast to acute tolerance during a binge, requires a longer interval between doses, usually about one day. Sensitization often occurs with stimulants such as cocaine or amphetamine, but also occurs with other drugs. * Cross tolerance occurs when repeated use of a drug in a given category confers tolerance not only to that drug but also to other drugs in the same pharmacological category, such as opioid receptor agonists. For example, a patient on methadone maintenance therapy might not experience analgesia elicited by morphine due to cross tolerance.

questions.question:
A patient presented with breathing difficulty and nasal polyposis when he took aspirin for fever. He faced this issue previously too when he took aspirin. Which among the following is not true about this?

COX -  Cyclooxygenase

Occur on exposure to only aspirin

questions.explanation:
The diagnosis for this patient with breathing difficulty and nasal polyposis, triggered by aspirin, a COX-1 inhibitor is aspirin-induced asthma, also known as Samter's triad. The statement that is not true is that "it occurs on exposure to only aspirin", as this condition can also be triggered by other NSAIDs that inhibit COX-1, and is not restricted to just aspirin alone.

Samter's triad is also known as aspirin-induced asthma or aspirin-sensitive asthma. It consists of:

  • Nasal polyposis
  • Bronchial asthma
  • Aspirin intolerance

A patient with Samter's triad experiences severe asthma and nasal polyposis triggered by aspirin or other COX-1 inhibitors. This condition involves nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, anosmia, and recurrent chronic rhinosinusitis, with acute asthma attacks often occurring a few hours after ingestion of these medications.

These patients overproduce leukotrienes due to COX-1 inhibition and decreased prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) levels. Therefore, they should avoid COX-1 inhibitors like aspirin and most NSAIDs but can generally tolerate COX-2 inhibitors and acetaminophen.

Treatment typically includes leukotriene modifiers, and in some cases, aspirin desensitization may be used to manage symptoms and allow the use of aspirin or NSAIDs if necessary for other conditions. Recent advances in treatment include biologics such as Dupilumab and IL-5 inhibitors, which are increasingly effective in managing aspirin-induced asthma and may replace aspirin desensitization except when ongoing aspirin or NSAID therapy is required.

Other options:

Option A: The reaction in aspirin-induced asthma is not due to an allergic sensitization but rather due to the inhibition of COX-1 and subsequent overproduction of leukotrienes.

Option B: Montelukast, a leukotriene receptor antagonist, is effective in managing symptoms of aspirin-induced asthma by counteracting the elevated levels of leukotrienes that contribute to inflammation and respiratory issues.

Option D: It occurs with exposure to other NSAIDs too, that block COX-1. Patients with aspirin-induced asthma can react to other NSAIDs that inhibit COX-1, not just aspirin.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A 75-year-old female presented with urinary incontinence. She also has cognition decline and dementia. Which of the following drugs is useful for treating urinary incontinence?
questions.explanation:
For managing urinary incontinence in a 75-year-old female with cognitive decline and dementia, tolterodine is useful.

Tolterodine is a muscarinic receptor antagonist specifically effective for treating urinary incontinence. It exhibits selectivity for the urinary bladder, which helps to minimize side effects compared to other antimuscarinic agents. This selectivity is beneficial for patients with cognitive decline or dementia, as it reduces the risk of adverse effects. Tolterodine is metabolized by CYP2D6, so its dosage may need adjustment based on individual CYP2D6 activity, making it a suitable option for managing urinary incontinence while minimizing potential side effects.

Other muscarinic antagonists for urinary incontinence include oxybutynin, trospium chloride, darifenacin, solifenacin, and fesoterodine. Oxybutynin, though effective, often causes antimuscarinic side effects such as xerostomia. Trospium chloride, being a quaternary amine, is better tolerated and excreted primarily via the kidneys, requiring dosage adjustments in renal impairment. Darifenacin and solifenacin have selectivity for M3 receptors, which helps balance efficacy and side effects, while fesoterodine, a prodrug, provides a stable pharmacokinetic profile due to its conversion to tolterodine’s active metabolite.

Other Options:

Option A: Tiotropium and Option C: Ipratropium are muscarinic antagonists used primarily for respiratory conditions such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and asthma, rather than urinary incontinence. Tiotropium is a long-acting agent with selectivity for M1 and M3 receptors, while Ipratropium is used more frequently for its short-acting effects.

Option D: Telenzepine, an analogue of Pirenzepine, displays higher potency and selectivity for M1 receptors compared to pirenzepine and is used in treating acid-peptic disease, not urinary incontinence.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A hypertensive patient with chronic kidney disease was having frequent attacks of renal colic. Which of the following diuretics is used?
questions.explanation:
For a hypertensive patient with chronic kidney disease experiencing frequent attacks of renal colic, hydrochlorothiazide, a thiazide diuretic, is often used.

Thiazide diuretics are particularly effective in cases of calcium oxalate kidney stones because they reduce urinary calcium excretion. They work by acting on the distal convoluted tubule (DCT) of the nephron, where they inhibit the Na+/Cl- co-transporter. This inhibition decreases the intracellular sodium concentration, which, through compensatory mechanisms, leads to increased calcium reabsorption into the bloodstream.

While this mechanism helps in decreasing urinary calcium and managing calcium oxalate stones, thiazide diuretics can also cause adverse effects such as hypokalemia, hyperuricemia, and hypercalcemia. The increased reabsorption of uric acid due to the diuretic effect can exacerbate conditions like gout and should be monitored carefully.

In addition to their use in treating calcium oxalate kidney stones, thiazide diuretics are commonly prescribed for managing uncomplicated hypertension and treating edema associated with heart, liver, and kidney diseases. They are also used for conditions like osteoporosis and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. 

Other options:

Option A: Furosemide is a diuretic that can increase calcium excretion, potentially raising PTH as the body tries to conserve calcium.

Option B: Osmotic diuretics, like mannitol, retain water isoosmotically in the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) and descending loop of Henle which are freely permeable to water. Luminal fluid is diluted and opposes NaCl reabsorption and promotes calcium excretion. They are indicated in raised intracranial tension and in dialysis disequilibrium.

Option D: Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic and aldosterone antagonist. It works by competitively inhibiting aldosterone receptors in the distal tubules of the kidney.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: Which of the following beta-adrenergic blockers are beneficial for patients with reduced ejection fraction and can reduce mortality in chronic heart failure without causing exacerbations over a few years?
questions.explanation:
The beta-adrenergic blocker that is useful in patients with reduced ejection fraction and can reduce mortality in chronic heart failure without causing exacerbations over a few years is bisoprolol.

Bisoprolol is preferred for use in patients having heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF).

The exacerbation mentioned in the context of beta-blockers for heart failure refers to the potential worsening of heart failure symptoms in some patients, despite the overall benefits of these medications. They can sometimes lead to a decline in left ventricular function, particularly in individuals with limited cardiac reserve who rely heavily on adrenergic stimulation. This deterioration can manifest as increased heart failure symptoms or a decrease in cardiac function. The only beta-blockers that have been proven to improve the survival of patients with HFrEF or chronic HF are -

  • Bisoprolol
  • Metoprolol
  • Carvedilol

HFrEF is a complex clinical syndrome where the ventricle fails to adequately fill with or eject blood, typically defined by an ejection fraction (EF) less than or equal to 40%. Key etiologies include coronary artery disease, valvular heart disease, congenital heart diseases, and autoimmune diseases like giant cell myocarditis. Patients with HFrEF commonly experience symptoms like dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and may present with pedal edema, elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP), ascites, and hepatomegaly on examination.

The pharmacological management of HFrEF involves drugs with both symptomatic and mortality benefits, including Angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitors (ARNIs) such as sacubitril/valsartan, angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors like ramipril and enalapril, β-blockers such as metoprolol and carvedilol, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists like spironolactone and eplerenone, sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors like dapagliflozin, and hydralazine plus isosorbide dinitrate (noting a mortality benefit specifically in African-American patients). Drugs used primarily for symptomatic relief, such as loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide), and digoxin, are reserved for specific indications or during decompensation. Non-pharmacological therapies for HFrEF include implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICD) and cardiac resynchronization therapy.

questions.question: Which drug is used for maintenance therapy in opium addiction?

The drug used among the following options for maintenance therapy in opium addiction is buprenorphine.

Buprenorphine is a partial μ-opioid agonist and an antagonist at δ and κ receptors. It is widely used both as an analgesic for chronic pain conditions, such as cancer pain, and as a treatment for opioid dependence, serving as an alternative to methadone.

It effectively controls cravings and blocks the effects of higher-efficacy opioids. It is often administered in combination with naloxone to prevent misuse, although it may be given alone to pregnant women or individuals with naloxone allergies. Initial dosing typically starts at 2-4 mg daily, with adjustments made to stabilize the dose at approximately 12 to 16 mg/day. 

For opioid use disorder, effective management includes both withdrawal and long-term treatment strategies. Withdrawal and detoxification generally start with managing physical dependence using medications like methadone or buprenorphine. Methadone, a full agonist, is used to stabilize and reduce withdrawal symptoms, while buprenorphine helps with cravings and has a lower risk of overdose.

Clonidine and lofexidine, alpha-2 agonists, are used to ameliorate withdrawal symptoms. Lofexidine, approved by the FDA, is the first non-opioid treatment specifically for opioid withdrawal in adults. Naltrexone, a long-acting opioid antagonist, is used as an adjunct in patients who are already opioid-free; however, it will precipitate acute withdrawal symptoms if administered to those still dependent on opioids.

questions.question: A patient who recently underwent surgery has complaints of nausea and vomiting. He was prescribed a drug called aprepitant. What is its mechanism of action?
questions.explanation:
The class of drugs most preferred in patients suffering from postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV), following surgery are the NK1 antagonists like aprepitant.

Substance P is a neuropeptide that interacts with neurokinin-1 (NK-1) receptors. NK1 antagonists inhibit substance P at central and peripheral receptors. Aprepitant, fosaprepitant are examples of NK1 antagonists. It also acts on the chemotrigger zone whose location is shown below.



PONV Physiology: Afferents from the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ), vagal neurons in the gastrointestinal system, neurons from the vestibular system and midbrain afferents relay within the vomiting centre in the reticular formation of the brainstem which then project into the nucleus tractus solitarius.

Risk factors for PONV are divided into:

  • Patient factors
    • Female>male
    • Age<50 years
    • Prior history of motion sickness
    • Non-smokers > smokers (CTZ is desensitized)
  • Preoperative factors

questions.question:
A patient is started on a 3 HP TPT regimen. Which of the following is true regarding the regimen?

TPT - Tuberculosis Preventative Therapy
options: There is more compliance in 3HP than 9H and 6H
Chance of abortion in 3 HP is same as 6H
3HP regimen is less effective than 6H and 9H in preventing active TB
questions.correct_answer: There is more compliance in 3HP than 9H and 6H
questions.explanation:
The 3HP regimen, which involves once-weekly doses of Isoniazid and Rifapentine for 12 weeks, has been found to have higher patient compliance than the 9-month regimen of Isoniazid (9H) and the 6-month regimen (6H).

The shorter duration and reduced number of doses in the 3HP regimen make it more convenient and thus lead to better adherence. Studies have shown that patients are more likely to complete the 3HP regimen due to the shorter treatment duration and lower pill burden.

TPT stands for Tuberculosis Preventive Therapy. It is a treatment given to individuals who are at high risk of developing active tuberculosis (TB) to prevent the progression from latent TB infection (where the person is infected with the TB bacteria but does not have symptoms) to active TB disease.

There are different regimens for TPT, including:

  • 3HP: A regimen consisting of once-weekly doses of Isoniazid (H) and Rifapentine (P) for 12 weeks.
  • 6H: A regimen consisting of daily Isoniazid for 6 months.
  • 9H: A regimen consisting of daily Isoniazid for 9 months.

TPT is particularly important for individuals with latent TB who have a higher risk of developing active TB, such as those with HIV, close contacts of TB patients, or those with certain medical conditions that weaken the immune system.

Other options: 

Option B: Research has demonstrated that the 3HP regimen offers better compliance and similar effectiveness compared to the traditional 6H and 9H regimens. The shorter duration of 3HP (once weekly for 12 weeks) makes it more convenient and tolerable for patients, which leads to higher adherence rates. Thus, there is a significant difference in patient compliance between these regimens, with 3HP showing clear advantages.

Option C: Although 3HP is generally considered safe, data suggests that the risk profile for adverse effects, including potential reproductive impacts like abortion, differs between regimens. Specifically, 6H may have a different side effect profile due to the prolonged exposure to the drug over six months, compared to the shorter and intermittent dosing of 3HP. 

Option D: Studies have confirmed that the 3HP regimen is as effective as 6H and 9H in preventing active tuberculosis (TB). Both regimens aim to prevent latent TB from progressing to active disease, and 3HP has been shown to achieve similar outcomes with fewer doses, enhancing patient compliance.

questions.question: A female suffered a head injury from a road traffic accident. On examination, there is elevated intracranial pressure. Which diuretic among the following can be used in her condition?

In this patient with raised intracranial pressure after a road traffic accident, mannitol is the diuretic of choice in her management to reduce intracranial pressure. 

Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic that draws fluid out of the brain tissue and into the bloodstream as it forms a hypertonic solution when it reaches the bloodstream, thereby reducing intracranial pressure (ICP). It is commonly used in cases of traumatic brain injury or other conditions that cause elevated ICP. This effect helps to relieve pressure on the brain, preventing further damage.

Other options: 

The other diuretics listed Hydrochlorothiazide, Spironolactone, and Acetazolamide are not typically used for managing elevated ICP. They are not hypertonic solutes and thus do not lead to a rapid reduction of the ICP as mannitol does.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A 2-year-old child presents to the emergency department with lethargy, difficulty feeding, and dehydration. His vitals are stable and his ECG is shown below. What is the next step in his management?
questions.explanation:
This clinical history along the EKG showing narrow QRS complexes without P waves and pseudo R waves in aVR lead suggests paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT) and the next step in his management would be an initial dose of adenosine at 0.1 mg/kg.

PSVT is a regular, narrow QRS complex tachycardia, most often caused due to an atrioventricular nodal re-entrant circuit. Patients may present with sudden onset palpitations, dizziness, and diaphoresis. 

Management involves slowing AV node conduction and vagal maneuvers (e.g., Valsalva maneuver, splashing cold water on the face) are the first step. If this does not work, intravenous (IV) adenosine is the drug of choice used to terminate the majority of PSVT episodes.

Adenosine is a very short-acting endogenous purine signal molecule. It is administered as a 6 mg IV bolus over 2-3 seconds followed by a rapid flush with 20 mL NS. It can be followed up with a 12 mg IV bolus dose if required. It causes membrane hyperpolarization of cardiac muscle cells to terminate the re-entrant circuit through the AV node.

Since the action of the drug lasts for less than a minute, adverse effects are short-lived. These include transient shortness of breath, chest pain, hypotension, and cutaneous flushing due to vasodilation. It can however precipitate bronchospasm in asthmatics and verapamil is preferred in such patients.



When the patient is hemodynamically unstable, i.e., hypotension with unconsciousness or respiratory distress, QRS-synchronous direct current cardioversion is done.

questions.question: Which of the following reasons best explains the combination of Atropine (0.025 mg) and Diphenoxylate (2.5 mg) for treating secretory diarrhoea?

Diphenoxylate is an opioid agonist primarily used as an antidiarrheal agent. It works by slowing down intestinal motility, allowing more time for water and electrolytes to be absorbed from the intestines, which helps reduce diarrhea. questions.question: A hypertensive patient is started on a drug to control his BP. He had complaints of dry mouth, drowsiness, and confusion after taking this drug, but he still continued to take the drug for 1 year. questions.explanation:
The adverse effects seen in this patient and the presentation of rebound hypertension on sudden drug withdrawal indicate that the drug is clonidine. 

Clonidine is an alpha-2 receptor agonist and a centrally-acting antihypertensive agent. It treats high blood pressure by stimulating presynaptic α2 receptors in the vasomotor center in the brainstem. This binding has a sympatholytic effect, by suppressing the release of norepinephrine and other sympathomimetics.

Abrupt withdrawal after long-term therapy can result in rebound hypertension, restlessness, and sympathetic overactivity. Dry mouth and sedation are the major side effects of clonidine. It can also cause impotency and constipation. Rebound hypertension is a potentially serious complication and occurs if the drug is missed for 1–2 days. This is associated with an alarming rise in blood pressure which may be more than the pretreatment level.

Phentolamine is used for the control of hypertension due to clonidine withdrawal.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: In which phase of clinical trials is drug dosing done?
questions.explanation:
The dosing of a new drug is tested in phase I of a clinical trial.

Phase I trials are usually performed on healthy volunteers to check the safety and pharmacokinetic properties of a drug. The participants in this phase do not gain any direct health benefits from taking part. They are generally paid a fee for their time, with the payments being regulated and not related to the risk involved.

In clinical trials, drug dosing typically occurs in Phase I, where researchers establish the optimal dose to achieve desired effects while minimizing side effects. In these phases, they focus on safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics.

Dose-ranging, primarily conducted in Phase II trials, involves testing multiple doses to identify the most effective and safe dose range. This phase helps determine the minimum effective dose and maximum tolerated dose, providing critical data for subsequent studies in Phase 3, where the chosen dose is tested for efficacy and safety in a larger population.

questions.question: A patient with a gynecological malignancy is started on Methotrexate. Later she develops oral and gastric ulcers. Which nucleotide synthesis is affected in her?
questions.explanation:
TMP synthesis is affected due to methotrexate. 

Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), which is required to synthesize tetrahydrofolate. Tetrahydrofolate is essential for converting dUMP to dTMP (thymidine monophosphate) in the nucleotide synthesis pathway. Therefore, the nucleotide synthesis affected in this patient is TMP (thymidine monophosphate).

By inhibiting DHFR, methotrexate reduces the availability of THF, thereby disrupting the production of thymidylate (TMP), which is necessary for DNA replication and repair. This disruption leads to impaired DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells, such as cancer cells. However, it also affects other rapidly dividing cells, including those in the gastrointestinal tract and oral mucosa, leading to side effects like oral and gastric ulcers.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A male patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) was prescribed theophylline. He noticed that his urine output had increased the following day. This action of the drug is mediated through which of the following receptors?
questions.explanation:
An increased urine output after administering theophylline is due to the antagonism at adenosine A1 receptors.

The adenosine A1 receptors are present in the afferent arteriole of the glomeruli. When activated, they cause vasoconstriction that reduces the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and renal blood flow. This reduces urine output. Antagonistic action on these receptors will cause an increased GFR and renal blood flow and hence increased urine output.

Methylxanthines like theophylline and aminophylline are the bronchodilators used mainly in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and bronchial asthma. The pharmacological actions of theophylline are:

  • It inhibits phosphodiesterase (PDE) non-selectively, thereby increasing cellular cAMP and cGMP, causing bronchodilation. 
  • Adenosine causes bronchoconstriction by releasing histamine and leukotrienes. Theophylline antagonizes adenosine A1 receptors and causes bronchodilation.
  • It increases IL-10 release, which has anti-inflammatory actions.
  • It causes a decrease in gene transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines.
  • It promotes apoptosis of granulocytes and thereby, reduces the inflammatory load in the airways.

Adverse effects of theophylline:

  • Headache, nausea, and vomiting (due to inhibition of PDE4)
  • Increased acid secretion (due to PDE inhibition)
  • Diuresis (due to inhibition of adenosine A1 receptors)
  • Cardiac arrhythmias (due to inhibition of cardiac PDE3 and antagonism of cardiac A1 receptors).
  • Seizures (due to central A1 receptor antagonism).

Theophylline is mainly metabolized mainly by the enzyme CYP1A2. Therefore, it has various drug interactions, which include:

  1. Agents that lower its plasma level are smoking, phenytoin, rifampicin, and phenobarbitone.
  2. Drugs that increase its plasma level are erythromycin, ciprofloxacin, oral contraceptives, and allopurinol.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A patient with deep vein thrombosis was started on a new drug. After 2 days, he presented with the given finding. Which of the following drugs is implicated in causing the above condition?
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario of the development of purple toe syndrome, after starting a new drug for the treatment of deep vein thrombosis, is suggestive of the adverse effect of warfarin.

Purple toe syndrome is a rare complication of warfarin therapy. It occurs due to cholesterol microemboli released from atheromatous plaques, which cause arteriolar occlusion. Warfarin must be immediately stopped and replaced with an oral factor Xa inhibitor (e.g. apixaban).

Activation of coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X and proteins C and S are done by carboxylation of their glutamate residues, with the help of the reduced form of vitamin K as a co-factor. This reduced form of vitamin K needs to be constantly recycled back from its oxidized form for the reaction to continue. This recycling is done by the enzyme vitamin K epoxide reductase, which is competitively inhibited by warfarin. Hence, there will be a reduction in the activation of coagulation factors.

The image below shows warfarin's mechanism of action.



The half-life of proteins C and S are 8 and 24 hours, respectively, which is relatively shorter than the half-lives of other clotting factors, particularly factor II. Therefore, the full antithrombotic effect of warfarin is not achieved for 4 to 5 days. For this reason, warfarin must be bridged with a rapidly acting parenteral anticoagulant, such as heparin, low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH), or fondaparinux, in patients with thrombosis or at high risk for thrombosis.

Uses of warfarin are acute deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and preventing stroke or systemic embolization in patients with a mechanical heart valve. 

Adverse effects of warfarin are bleeding, skin necrosis, purple toe syndrome, and fetal warfarin syndrome (hypoplasia of the nose, eye socket, hand bones, and growth retardation).

The therapeutic dose of warfarin is monitored by an INR range of 2-3. Warfarin toxicity can occur when the INR exceeds 4 and can lead to fatal bleeding. Treatment includes withholding warfarin, with vitamin K, and blood transfusions or fresh frozen plasma to replenish clotting factors.

Warfarin, LMWH, and UFH do not accumulate in breast milk and do not have an anticoagulant effect in the newborn. They are compatible with breastfeeding.

Warfarin is mainly metabolized by the CYP2C9 enzyme. Drugs that affect the CYP2C9 enzyme can alter the anticoagulant function of warfarin and these include the following:

Reduced efficacy:

  • CYP2C9 activation by drugs: barbiturates, carbamazepine, rifampin
  • Oral contraceptives: increase blood levels of clotting factors

Increased efficacy:

  • Drugs causing CYP2C9 inhibition:
    • Amiodarone
    • Azole antifungals
    • Cimetidine
    • Clopidogrel
    • Cotrimoxazole
    • Disulfiram
    • Isoniazid
    • Metronidazole
    • Fluoxetine
    • Sulfinpyrazone
    • Zafirlukast

Other options:

Option B: Heparin acts by activating antithrombin III, thereby inactivating the active form of clotting factors II, IX, X, XI, XII, and XIII. Adverse effects are bleeding and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) due to the formation of antibodies against the heparin-platelet complex.

Option C: Dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor. It is used for the prevention of embolism and stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation. Bleeding and dyspepsia are the most important adverse effects.

Option D: Rivaroxaban is a direct inhibitor of factor Xa. It is used for prophylaxis and treatment of deep vein thrombosis. Side effects reported are bleeding, nausea, hypotension, tachycardia, and edema.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A patient undergoing chemotherapy was given an antiemetic, after which he developed symptoms like acute dystonia, bradykinesia, and tremors. Which of the following drugs would have caused these symptoms?
questions.explanation:
In the above scenario, the patient has developed extrapyramidal adverse effects like acute dystonia, bradykinesia, and tremors. This is likely due to the antagonist action on dopamine receptors by metoclopramide.

Metoclopramide is a prokinetic and antiemetic. It has the following pharmacological actions:

  • Dopamine receptor antagonist 
  • Serotonin (5HT4) receptor agonist 
  • Serotonin (5HT3) antagonist
  • Sensitization of muscarinic receptors on smooth muscle. This results in increased lower esophageal sphincter tone and stimulates gastric antral contractions.

Metoclopramide acts on both the gastrointestinal system and central nervous system. It is used as an upper antiemetic for many types of vomiting, especially migraine, drug-induced, and chemotherapy-induced. It is also used as a prokinetic in gastroparesis to increase gastric emptying.

Adverse effects of metoclopramide are mainly extrapyramidal effects, and these include acute dystonia, Parkinson-like symptoms (tremors, bradykinesia, rigidity), tardive dyskinesia, galactorrhea due to hyperprolactinemia, and methemoglobinemia in neonates.

Extrapyramidal symptoms can be treated by discontinuation of metoclopramide and administration of anticholinergics or antihistaminics.

Other options:

Option A: Ondansetron is a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist. It blocks impulses at the peripheral origin in GIT. It is most commonly indicated for the treatment of postoperative and chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. Headache and dizziness are the common adverse effects.

Option C: Meclizine is a long-acting H1 antihistaminic drug. It is used for seasickness. It is less sedative and less anticholinergic.

Option D: Scopolamine (hyoscine) is a muscarinic antagonist. It blocks neural pathways from the vestibular apparatus in the inner ear to the emetic center in the brainstem. A transdermal patch of scopolamine is used as an antiemetic in motion sickness. Constipation, drowsiness, dry mouth, and blurred vision are the common adverse effects.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A young patient started to take a weight loss medication that acts by inhibiting fat absorption from food. After a few weeks, she developed easy bruising and increased menstrual bleeding. Deficiency of which of the following vitamins is responsible for her condition?
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario of easy bruising and increased menstrual bleeding following weight loss medication that inhibits fat absorption from food is suggestive of vitamin K deficiency.

Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin. Hence, drugs that inhibit the absorption of fat (eg; ezetimibe) also inhibit the absorption of fat-soluble vitamin K. The following are the vitamers of vitamin K:

  • Phylloquinone (Vitamin K1) is the normal dietary source of Vitamin K that is found in green vegetables.
  • Menaquinone (Vitamin K2) is synthesized by intestinal bacteria.
  • Menadione (Vitamin K3) is a synthetic compound that is metabolized to phylloquinone.

Vitamin K is required for γ-carboxylation of glutamate residues of clotting factors like prothrombin (factor II), factors VII, IX, and X. Warfarin inhibits γ-carboxylation by preventing the conversion of vitamin K to its active hydroquinone form.

Vitamin K deficiency in adults may be seen in patients with liver disease, obstructive jaundice, malabsorption, and prolonged antimicrobial therapy. Vitamin K deficiency is usually diagnosed on the basis of an elevated prothrombin time or reduced clotting factors. 

Vitamin K deficiency is treated with a parenteral dose of 10 mg followed by 5mg (duration depends on the severity of vitamin K deficiency).

Other options:

Option A: Vitamin E is a fat-soluble vitamin. The levels of vitamin E also will get decreased following taking weight loss medication that inhibits fat absorption from food. But the symptoms of vitamin E deficiency include hemolytic anemia and neuromuscular manifestations.

Option C: Vitamin B6 is a water-soluble vitamin. Drugs that cause vitamin B6 deficiency are isoniazid, hydralazine, cycloserine, penicillamine, and oral contraceptives. Patients usually present with peripheral neuritis, anemia, seborrheic dermatitis, glossitis, lowered seizure threshold, or convulsions (due to fall in brain GABA levels).

Option D: Vitamin D is a fat-soluble vitamin. Vitamin D levels will also decrease following weight loss medication that inhibits fat absorption from food. Patients with vitamin D deficiency will typically develop rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A woman presenting with symptoms of urinary tract infection was prescribed a drug that causes tendon rupture and arthropathy. What is the mechanism of action of the drug?
questions.explanation:
In the above scenario, the antimicrobial prescribed for urinary tract infection, which has a propensity to cause tendon rupture and arthropathy, is likely to be a fluoroquinolone. The mechanism of action of the drug is DNA gyrase inhibition.

Normally, during replication, to prevent excessive positive supercoiling of the strands, DNA gyrase nicks double-stranded DNA and introduces negative supercoils. Fluoroquinolones, by inhibiting DNA gyrase (in gram-negative bacteria), result in the production of damaged DNA. This is finally digested by exonucleases, resulting in bactericidal action.

Fluoroquinolones inhibit topoisomerase IV in gram-positive bacteria.

Fluoroquinolones are used in the treatment of urinary tract infections, prostatitis, and gastrointestinal, respiratory infections, and as a second-line drug in anti-tubercular therapy. They are avoided in children and pregnant women.

Adverse effects of fluoroquinolones are arthralgia, tendon rupture, Clostridium difficile colitis, dysglycemia, prolonged QT interval, rashes, hallucinations, delirium, and seizures.

Other options:

Option B: Ribosomal inhibition is the mechanism of action of various antimicrobials like tetracyclines, aminoglycosides, chloramphenicol, and macrolides.

Option C: Cell wall synthesis inhibition is done by beta-lactam antibiotics.

Option D: Inhibition of folic acid synthesis is the mechanism of action of sulfonamides and co-trimoxazole.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A patient was brought to the emergency with a history of consumption of 8 tablets of digoxin. On examination, he was unstable and his heart rate was 56 bpm. ECG showed a 3rd-degree heart block. What is the next step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Administration of digibind (antibody against digoxin) is the next step in managing this patient. An unstable patient with bradycardia and 3rd-degree heart block following digoxin toxicity should be treated with digibind.

Digibind is a nonimmunogenic antibody used to treat cardiotoxicity due to digoxin. It is nonimmunogenic because it lacks the Fc fragment.

Digoxin is the cardiac glycoside used to treat heart failure and control ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation/flutter.

It inhibits Na+/K+ ATPase, a membrane-bound transporter to increase intracellular sodium. As a result, there is less expulsion of calcium from the cell by the sodium-calcium exchanger (NCX). Increased calcium inside the myocyte leads to an increase in cardiac contractility.

The most common cardiac manifestations of digitalis toxicity are ventricular tachycardia, partial to complete A-V block, severe bradycardia, and atrial fibrillation/flutter.

Factors that increase the risk of digoxin toxicity are:

  • Hypokalemia
  • Drugs that decrease digoxin elimination (inhibitors of P-glycoprotein) like quinidine
  • Renal/hepatic failure
  • Thyrotoxicosis

Option B: Lidocaine is commonly used as a local anesthetic. It has anti-arrhythmic properties and is used to suppress ventricular tachycardia caused by digitalis toxicity.

Option C: DC cardioversion is used for tachyarrythmias when pharmacologic treatment fails. It is not used in bradyarrhythmias.

Option D: Phenytoin is an antiepileptic used for the treatment of generalized tonic-clonic seizures and partial seizures. It can also be used for the treatment of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia due to QT prolongation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: An elderly man, who is a known case of diabetic nephropathy, presented to the emergency with palpitations and chest discomfort. ECG showed tall T-waves. Laboratory investigations showed elevated potassium levels. Which of the following drugs will cause the shift of potassium back into the cell?
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario with ECG showing tall T-waves and elevated serum potassium levels are suggestive of hyperkalemia. Epinephrine will cause the shift of potassium back into the cell.

Epinephrine is an agonist at alpha 1, beta 1, and beta 2 receptors.

The β actions are mediated through cAMP. Epinephrine binds to Gs → ATP and is broken down to cAMP by the enzyme adenylyl cyclase. This results in:

  • In the liver and muscle- hyperglycemia and hypokalemia due to potassium uptake in muscle and liver
  • In adipose tissue- increased plasma free fatty acids
  • In the heart- an increased force of contraction reinforces the positive inotropic action
  • In pancreatic islets- increases glucagon secretion

Epinephrine is used in anaphylaxis, to prolong the action of local anesthetics, cardiac arrest, and as inhalational epinephrine in the treatment of post-intubation and infectious croup.

Epinephrine is contraindicated in anesthesia with halothane due to the risk of arrhythmias and in patients receiving beta-blockers because a marked rise in BP can occur due to unopposed alpha action.

Hyperkalemia refers to an increase in the levels of serum potassium >5.5mEq/L.

The image given below shows sequential ECG changes seen in hyperkalemia.



Hyperkalemia is a medical emergency and has to be treated when ECG changes are present or severe hyperkalemia (serum K+ >6.5) without ECG changes. Management is as follows:

  • Intravenous infusion of 10 ml of 10% calcium gluconate for 2-3 minutes with cardiac monitoring. It helps to antagonize the cardiac effects.
  • Intravenous regular insulin 10 units followed by 50mL of 50 % dextrose. This helps in shifting the plasma K+ into the cells.
  • Nebulisation with β2 agonists such as albuterol or salbutamol.
  • Cation exchange resins, diuretics, and/or dialysis are useful to remove the excess potassium.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A patient with a pituitary tumor that overproduced growth hormone underwent surgical removal of the tumor. The resection was found to be incomplete. What is the first-line treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
The above scenario with a pituitary tumor producing growth hormone is likely to cause acromegaly in the patient. Octreotide is the first-line treatment for this condition.

Octreotide is a synthetic analog of somatostatin.

Octreotide can be used in the following conditions:

  • Acromegaly
  • Secretory diarrheas associated with carcinoid, AIDS, cancer chemotherapy, or diabetes- by suppression of hormones that enhance intestinal mucosal secretion.
  • Bleeding esophageal varices- reduces hepatic blood flow and helps stop bleeding.
  • Dumping syndrome in post gastric surgery patients

Adverse effects of octreotide are:

  • Abdominal pain
  • Nausea
  • Steatorrhea
  • Gall stones (due to biliary stasis)
  • Hyperglycemia

Other options:

Option A: Leuprolide is a long-acting GnRH agonist. It is used for palliation of carcinoma prostate, uterine fibroids, endometriosis, and precocious puberty. Side effects include hot flashes, decreased bone mineral density, vaginal dryness, and erectile dysfunction.

Option B: Goserelin is also a GnRH agonist used for the treatment of endometriosis, dysfunctional uterine bleeding, and for prostate and breast cancer.

Option C: Nafarelin is a long-acting GnRH agonist. It is used for the treatment of endometriosis, uterine fibroids, and central precocious puberty.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A middle-aged male patient presents with protrusion of the chin, excessive sweating, impaired glucose tolerance, and enlargement of hands and feet. Which of the following is a growth hormone receptor antagonist used to treat this condition?
questions.explanation:
The clinical features of protrusion of the chin, excessive sweating, impaired glucose tolerance, and enlargement of hands and feet are suggestive of acromegaly. Pegvisomant is a growth hormone receptor antagonist used to treat this condition.

Acromegaly is commonly caused due to growth hormone-secreting somatotroph adenoma. It occurs secondary to mutations of the pituitary-specific gene PIT-1.

Patients present with frontal bossing, increased hand and foot size, mandibular enlargement with prognathism, widened space between the lower incisor teeth, soft tissue swelling resulting in increased heel pad thickness, coarse facial features, and large fleshy nose.

Serum IGF-1 levels (elevated) and GH suppression test with oral glucose are useful in the diagnosis. The levels of GH do not reduce in response to the oral glucose load. 

Transsphenoidal surgical resection of the tumor, octreotide, and pegvisomant will be helpful in the management of this condition.

Other options:

Option A: Octreotide is a synthetic analog of somatostatin. It is used for the treatment of acromegaly and secretory diarrhea.

Option C: Cabergoline is a dopamine D2 receptor agonist. It is used as a first-line drug for the treatment of hyperprolactinemia.

Option D: Oglcegepant is a calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) antagonist. It is used for the treatment of migraine.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A diabetic patient presented with rhinitis and facial swelling. An intranasal biopsy revealed the presence of broad-based aseptate hyphae with branching at right angle. Evidence of vascular invasion was present.  What will be the drug of choice for this condition?
questions.explanation:
The above scenario and biopsy findings showing broad-based aseptate hyphae with branching at right angles are suggestive of mucormycosis. The drug of choice for mucormycosis is amphotericin B.

Mucormycosis is an opportunistic mycosis. It is typically seen in patients with diabetes mellitus and/or diabetic ketoacidosis and invades blood vessels.

The rhino-orbital-cerebral is the most common form of mucormycosis. Patients present with rhinitis, eye or facial pain, and facial numbness followed by the onset of conjunctival suffusion and swelling along with blurry vision.

Diagnosis is made by biopsy with histopathologic examination. The biopsy shows characteristic wide, ribbon-like aseptate hyphal elements that branch at right angles.

The below image shows biopsy findings seen in mucormycosis.



Treatment of the infection includes 4 steps:

  1. Initiation of therapy (amphotericin B) as early as possible.
  2. Surgical debridement.
  3. Reversal of underlying conditions and risk factors.
  4. Treatment of underlying malignancy if present.

Amphotericin B binds to ergosterol in the fungal membrane and forms pores or channels in the fungal cell membrane. This allows the leakage of cytosolic molecules and ions, leading to a loss of membrane integrity.

It is a broad-spectrum antifungal that can be used against Candida albicans, Cryptococcus neoformans, Blastomyces dermatitidis, Histoplasma capsulatum, Sporothrix schenckii, Coccidioides immitis, Aspergillus.

Amphotericin B also has antiprotozoal action along with antifungal properties and is effective against Leishmania.

Adverse effects of amphotericin B:

  • Infusion-related fever and chills
  • Azotemia/nephrotoxicity- all lipid formulations of amphotericin B are less nephrotoxic than conventional amphotericin B
  • Renal tubular acidosis 
  • Renal wasting of potassium and magnesium
  • Hypochromic normocytic anemia- due to decreased erythropoietin production from the kidney

Note: Mucormycosis recently emerged as an important superinfection in COVID-19 patients, especially in India. The surge in cases is most likely due to diabetes mellitus and steroid use.

Other options:

Option A: Fluconazole is used for the treatment of candidiasis and cryptococcosis.

Option C: Ketoconazole is used for both dermatophytosis and deep mycosis, but it has been replaced by itraconazole.

Option D: Griseofulvin is used for dermatophytosis. It is effective against the mycotic disease of the skin, hair, and nails due to Microsporum, Trichophyton, and Epidermophyton.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A tuberculosis patient on anti-tubercular treatment presents with a tingling sensation and paresthesia in the lower limbs. He is not a diabetic and occasionally consumes alcohol. Which of the following vitamins must be supplemented to this patient?
questions.explanation:
Vitamin B6 must be supplemented for this patient. The clinical features of tingling sensation and paresthesias in a patient on anti-tubercular treatment are suggestive of the adverse effect of isoniazid.

Isoniazid is the first-line antitubercular drug that inhibits the production of mycolic acid. It is a bactericidal drug against tubercle bacilli.

Adverse effects of isoniazid:

  • Peripheral neuritis (paresthesias, numbness, tingling sensation) due to interference with the production of active coenzyme pyridoxal phosphate from pyridoxine. Therefore, pyridoxine 10 mg/day (vitamin B6) is given prophylactically along with isoniazid to prevent neurotoxicity.
  • Hepatitis - isoniazid must be stopped at the first sign of hepatotoxicity.
  • Rashes
  • Anemia
  • Arthralgia

Toxicity of isoniazid results in metabolic acidosis and seizures. 

Note: Vitamin deficiency in alcoholics includes the following:

  • Folate causes megaloblastic anemia. It is treated by supplementation of oral doses of 5-15 mg of folic acid.
  • Vitamin B6 results in peripheral neuritis, anemia, and glossitis, and lowers the seizure threshold. It is treated by supplementation of oral doses of 2-5 mg of pyridoxine.
  • Thiamine results in Wernicke's encephalopathy. It is treated with 200 mg of intravenous thiamine three times daily, followed by 10 mg/day until complete recovery.
  • Vitamin A results in xerophthalmia and night blindness. It is treated with supplementation of oral vitamin A 3000-5000 IU/day.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: An elderly woman received a botox injection for the treatment of wrinkles. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of botulinum toxin?
options: Release of noradrenaline at synaptic cleft
Selectively and irreversibly inhibits nicotinic receptors
questions.explanation:
The botulinum toxin acts by inhibiting the release of acetylcholine into the synaptic cleft.

Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE protein, which is involved in the exocytosis of acetylcholine. Thus, it inhibits the release of acetylcholine.

The image given below shows the site of action of botulinum toxin:



This toxin causes a long-lasting loss of cholinergic transmission. Hence, it can be employed for the treatment of several spastic and neurological conditions caused by the overactivity of cholinergic nerves, such as age-related facial wrinkles, blepharospasm, spastic cerebral palsy, spasmodic torticollis, post-stroke spasticity, and axillary hyperhidrosis.

Adverse effects occur due to incorrect injection and overdose; they include ptosis, diplopia, facial swelling, dry mouth, muscle weakness, and respiratory paralysis.

Botulinum toxin is an exotoxin produced by the bacteria Clostridium botulinum. It is responsible for a type of food poisoning called botulism.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: Which of the following is a PCSK9 inhibitor?
questions.explanation:
Evolocumab is a PCSK9 inhibitor.

PCSK9 refers to proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9. They are mainly involved in the downregulation of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptors in the liver.

Evolocumab is a monoclonal antibody that inhibits PCSK-9 (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin). Inhibition of PCSK-9 prevents the degradation of LDL receptors and thus increases LDL-cholesterol clearance by the liver. They are used in patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) to decrease LDL levels.

Side effects of PCSK9 inhibitors are injection-site reactions, nasopharyngitis, urinary tract infection, and upper respiratory tract infection and it does not increase the risk of myopathy. 

Other options:

Option B: Ezetimibe inhibits cholesterol absorption by enterocytes in the small intestine. It lowers the total and LDL-C levels.

Option C: Bempedoic acid inhibits adenosine triphosphate-citrate lyase (ACL) and results in decreased LDL in patients not responding to statin therapy.

Option D: Clofibrate binds to PPAR-alpha and causes stimulation of fatty acid oxidation and increased LPL synthesis. This results in reduced triglycerides, LDL and increased high-density lipoprotein (HDL) levels. It causes myopathy when combined with statins and is associated with an increased risk of gallstone formation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: An elderly man presents with rigidity and tremors. On examination, he has blank facial expressions. Which of the following drugs can be used to manage this condition?
questions.explanation:
The clinical features of rigidity, tremors, and blank facial expressions are suggestive of Parkinson's disease. Monoamine oxidase-B (MAO-B) inhibitors like selegiline are used for the treatment of Parkinson disease.

Normally, MAO-B oxidizes dopamine. Selegiline is a selective and irreversible MAO-B inhibitor. Therefore, it increases dopamine levels in the brain. It is used as an adjuvant to levodopa in Parkinson's disease. It prolongs and enhances the action of levodopa.

Adverse effects of selegiline are postural hypotension, nausea, confusion, involuntary movements, and psychosis. Selegiline is contraindicated in patients with convulsive disorders.

Other options:

Option A: Clozapine is an atypical antipsychotic that selectively blocks dopamine (D4) receptors in the brain. It is used in the treatment of refractory schizophrenia. Agranulocytosis and metabolic syndrome are the important adverse effects.

Option B: Donepezil is a reversible cholinesterase inhibitor used for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease.

Option D: Haloperidol is a typical antipsychotic used for the treatment of acute schizophrenia, Huntington’s disease, and Gilles de la Tourette syndrome.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A 35-year-old chronic hypertensive woman visits the outpatient department for pre-conceptional counseling. Which of the following anti-hypertensives should she discontinue?
questions.explanation:
Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors should be discontinued in pregnancy as they can cause hypoplasia of organs, growth retardation, and fetal loss.

ACE inhibitors cause reduced perfusion and oligohydramnios leading to fetal growth retardation, calvarium maldevelopment, hypoplasia of lungs and kidneys, and limb contractures.

Antihypertensive drugs to be avoided in pregnancy:

  • ACE inhibitors and Angiotensin receptor blockers(ARB) - Can cause growth retardation and fetal damage.
  • Diuretics - Can decrease uteroplacental perfusion
  • Nonselective beta-blockers
  • Sodium nitroprusside - It is contraindicated in eclampsia.

  • Labetalol - Combined α + β blocker
  • Nifedipine - Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. It is useful in preeclampsia but should be stopped before labor as they weaken the uterine contractions.
  • Methyldopa
  • Hydralazine

Note:

Thiazide diuretics like hydrochlorothiazide are considered to be safe in pregnancy and are useful in the management of chronic hypertension in pregnant women.

questions.question: A pregnant woman was prescribed indomethacin. Which of the following effects does the drug have on the fetus?

questions.question: Which of the following can be prescribed in case of an open angle glaucoma with bronchial asthma?

questions.question: A patient started on antihypertensive presented with the following picture. Which of the following drugs is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
The image shows edema over the lips and face and its occurrence following intake of an antihypertensive is suggestive of drug-induced angioedema. Lisinopril being an ACE inhibitor is most likely to be responsible for this condition.

Angioedema with ACE inhibitors:

In very few patients(0.1%-0.5%), ACE inhibitors cause rapid swelling in the nose, throat, mouth, glottis, larynx, lips, or tongue. Once the drug is stopped symptoms improve drastically over hours. Angioedema of the intestine can occur very rarely. 

ACE inhibitor-associated angioedema is a class effect, and patients who develop this adverse event should not be prescribed any other drugs within the ACE inhibitor class.

Other adverse effects of ACE inhibitors:

Hypotension - A sudden fall in blood pressure can occur following the first dose of ACE inhibitors.

Cough - It can produce a bothersome dry cough due to the accumulation of bradykinin, substance P, or prostaglandins in the lungs. The cough usually disappears within 4 days of the stoppage of the drug.

Hyperkalemia due to K+ retention can occur.

Acute renal failure can occur with ACE inhibitors in patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis, stenosis of the artery to a single remaining kidney, heart failure, or volume depletion due to diarrhea or diuretics.

It should be discontinued in pregnant women as it can cause developmental defects.

It can also cause maculopapular skin rash in some cases.

Other options:

Option B: Nifedipine is a calcium channel blocker. Common adverse effects include headache, flushing, and dizziness. Peripheral edema may rarely occur.

Option C: Atenolol is a beta 1 selective antagonist. Bradycardia, fatigue, cold extremities are common adverse effects. CNS side effects like nightmares and depression are less frequent with atenolol than other beta-blockers.

Option D: Clonidine is an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist. The main adverse effects of clonidine are dry mouth and sedation. Bradycardia and sexual dysfunction are other effects.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A patient on aspirin presented with occult blood in the stool. This is due to inhibition of____ by aspirin
questions.explanation:
Aspirin causes inhibition of cyclooxygenase-1(COX-1) which would inhibit the formation of thromboxane A2. Thromboxane A2 is an inducer of platelet aggregation and is a potent vasoconstrictor. Hence inhibition of its formation is responsible for the bleeding complications of aspirin.

Aspirin is a noncompetitive, irreversible inhibitor of the cyclooxygenase(COX) enzyme. It is a nonselective COX inhibitor and inhibits both COX-1 and COX-2. 

Uses of aspirin:

  • Analgesic and antipyretic uses.
  • Acute rheumatic fever
  • Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Post myocardial infarction and stroke due to its antiplatelet action.
  • Prevention of preeclampsia

Adverse effects:

Nausea, vomiting, epigastric discomfort, and increased occult blood in stools are seen with analgesic doses(0.5-2g/day). Antiinflammatory doses(3-5g/day) can produce salicylism characterized by dizziness, tinnitus, vertigo, hyperventilation, reversible loss of hearing and vision, etc. It can cause elevation of liver enzymes and hepatic damage. Hypersensitivity reactions are also seen.

Reye's syndrome is a rare condition that can occur when salicylates like aspirin are given in children having viral infections like influenza.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A 60-year-old postmenopausal female patient with a previous history of Colle's fracture came with complaints of lower backache. On evaluation, her T score was -2.5. Which of the following statements are false about the management of her condition?
options: Teriparatide should be started before supplementing with bisphosphonates
Bisphosphonates are not given for more than a year
Calcium requirement is 1200 mg per day
Oral vitamin D3 is given along with oral calcium
questions.correct_answer: Bisphosphonates are not given for more than a year
questions.explanation:
Bisphosphonates are given for periods of more than one year (Option B is false). In this case, as the patient is having a history of osteoporotic fracture, teriparatide can be given before bisphosphonates.

Pharmacologic management of osteoporosis:

Bisphosphonates: These are pyrophosphate analogs that act by directly inhibiting bone resorption. The antiresorptive action is mainly due to its direct inhibitory effect on osteoclasts. It causes osteoclast apoptosis as well as the prevention of hydroxyapatite dissolution. Long-term bisphosphonates therapy is given for durations of 3-5 years, depending on the fracture risk of the patient. Since they are associated with osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femur fractures, a drug holiday may be advised after long-term management.

Teriparatide is a recombinant PTH analog that has an anabolic effect on bone homeostasis by increasing osteoblastic activity. It increases bone mineral density and decreases the risk of fractures in postmenopausal women. Indications of teriparatide therapy include the history of osteoporotic fracture, multiple risk factors for fracture, intolerance, or failure of previous osteoporosis therapy. It is only approved for 2 years of use. Clinical trials that used teriparatide prior to bisphosphonate have been proven effective.

Denosumab is a human monoclonal antibody with a mechanism of action similar to that of osteoprotegerin (OPG). It binds to RANK Ligand (RANKL), thereby inhibiting its binding to the RANK receptor of the surface of osteoclasts. This prevents RANK receptor activation and subsequent bone resorption.

Selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) - Estrogen has a protective effect that prevents accelerated bone loss. This is carried out by reducing the bone resorption effects of parathyroid hormone (PTH). Keeping in line with these effects, osteoporosis prevention in postmenopausal women has been attributed to the use of SERMs such as raloxifene. It acts as an estrogen agonist on the bone and liver.

Calcium and Vitamin D supplementation: Calcium supplementation in the elderly suppresses bone turnover and improves bone mineral density. 1200mg of calcium is daily required in adults of more than 50 years of age. Vitamin D supplementation with 400-800IU/day improves intestinal calcium absorption, suppresses bone remodeling, and improves bone mineral density.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A patient presented with a history of multiple episodes of vomiting. He was given an intravenous drug, and later, he developed abnormal movements. Which of the following can be used to treat him?
questions.explanation:
Benzhexol should be used in the management of this patient. The development of abnormal movements following an anti-emetic injection suggests that the antiemetic used in this case is probably metoclopramide.

Metoclopramide is a dopamine receptor antagonist used as a prokinetic and anti-emetic agent. It can produce extrapyramidal side effects and dystonia is seen acutely following intravenous injections. Anticholinergics like benzhexol (trihexyphenidyl) are used in the management of these side effects. Benzhexol is a centrally-acting anticholinergic agent. It acts by restoring the cholinergic balance in the striatal interneurons.

Extrapyramidal side effects of metoclopramide are commonly seen in children and young adults with higher doses. Acute dystonia occurs after intravenous administration, while parkinsonian-like symptoms develop weeks after therapy. It is managed with the discontinuation of metoclopramide and with anticholinergics or antihistaminics. Irreversible tardive dyskinesia can occur with chronic treatment.

Other adverse effects:

It can cause galactorrhea by its dopamine antagonism. Methemoglobinemia can occur if used in infants.

Other options:

Option A: Hyoscine (scopolamine): It is a muscarinic receptor antagonist used in the management of motion sickness and vomiting.

Option B: Cyproheptadine is an H1 receptor antagonist used in the management of various allergy-related conditions like allergic rhinitis, anaphylaxis, urticaria, etc.

Option C: Levodopa is the precursor of dopamine and it is given in combination with carbidopa for the management of parkinsonism.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: What formula is the dosing rate of a drug based on?
questions.explanation:
The formula for drug dosing rate is clearance x plasma concentration.

The equation for dose rate given here is based on steady-state concentration. When a drug is given repeatedly at short intervals it will accumulate in the body until the elimination of the drug matches its input. So steady-state concentration is the plasma concentration at which the drug elimination and drug input balance each other.

Steady-state concentration(Cpss) = Dose rate / Clearance

From this equation dose rate for a target steady-state plasma concentration is calculated as 

Dose rate = Clearance(CL) x target plasma concentration(Cpss)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A patient on digoxin, potassium chloride, clarithromycin, atenolol, and triamterene developed atrial fibrillation with controlled ventricular rate. Serum digoxin levels were raised. Which of his medications is responsible for the same?
questions.explanation:
Elevated serum digoxin levels and the development of atrial fibrillation with controlled ventricular rate are suggestive of digoxin toxicity. Clarithromycin when given along with digoxin can cause digoxin toxicity.

P-glycoprotein pumps play a major role in the elimination of digoxin. Drugs that inhibit P-glycoprotein can thereby decrease the elimination of digoxin and lead to digoxin toxicity. Macrolide antibiotics like clarithromycin and erythromycin are inhibitors of the P-glycoprotein. So clarithromycin when given along with digoxin can cause digoxin toxicity.

Other drugs that inhibit P-glycoprotein are - Amiodarone, quinidine, verapamil, diltiazem, cyclosporine, itraconazole, propafenone, and flecainide.

Digoxin is one of the cardiac glycosides which is derived from the digitalis plant and used clinically.

It inhibits Na+/K+ ATPase, a membrane-bound transporter to increase intracellular sodium. As a result, there is less expulsion of calcium from the cell by sodium-calcium exchanger (NCX). Increased calcium inside the myocyte leads to an increase in cardiac contractility.

The most common cardiac manifestations of digitalis toxicity include atrioventricular junctional rhythm, premature ventricular depolarizations, ventricular bigeminy, ventricular tachycardia, and second-degree AV blockade.

Factors that increase the risk of digoxin toxicity are:

  • Hypercalcemia
  • Hypomagnesemia
  • Hypokalemia- It increases the binding of the digoxin to the Na+/K+ ATPase pump. 
  • Drugs causing hypokalemia- loop and thiazide diuretics, amphotericin B, corticosteroids
  • Drugs that decrease digoxin elimination (inhibitors of P-glycoprotein)
  • Renal failure
  • Hypothyroidism

 Triamterene, atenolol, and potassium chloride cause hyperkalemia, and therefore do not cause digoxin toxicity.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question:
What is the mechanism of action of methotrexate in osteosarcoma?

UMP- Uridine monophosphate

DHFR- Dihydrofolate reductase
questions.explanation:
The anticancer activity of methotrexate is by inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR).

Methotrexate belongs to the antimetabolite class of anticancer drugs. The antifolate action of the drug is responsible for its anti-cancer properties.

Mechanism of action:

It is a folic acid analog and binds to the active catalytic site of dihydrofolate reductase(DHFR). This would inhibit the formation of tetrahydrofolate(THF) which is needed for purine nucleotides, thymidylate, and the amino acids serine and methionine. This would interfere with the production of DNA, RNA, and important cellular proteins.

Low doses of methotrexate are used in the management of rheumatic diseases. It is due to the inhibition of amino-imidazole carboxamide ribonucleotide (AICAR) transformylase and thymidylate synthetase. This results in increased levels of adenosine that inhibits inflammation.



Adverse effects:

Common side effects are nausea and mucosal ulcers. Others include anemia, leukopenia, stomatitis, GI ulcerations, and alopecia. Dose-related hepatotoxicity is also seen. The GI effects and hepatotoxicity can be reduced by the use of leucovorin or folinic acid.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question:
What should not be consumed by patients with bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis on metronidazole?

MAOI-Monoamine oxidase inhibitor

SSRI- Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor
questions.explanation:
Alcohol should not be consumed by a patient on metronidazole. Metronidazole produces a disulfiram-like reaction. If the patient consumes alcohol during or within 3 days of therapy, they may experience abdominal distress, vomiting, headache, and flushing. 

Disulfiram and disulfiram-like reactions:

Disulfiram inhibits the aldehyde dehydrogenase(ALDH) activity and thereby increases the concentration of acetaldehyde in the blood. When a person treated with disulfiram consumes alcohol he or she would develop symptoms of acetaldehyde poisoning. The symptoms are:

  • Flushing
  • Pulsating headache
  • Nausea and vomiting
  • Sweating
  • Tachycardia
  • Hypotension
  • Orthostatic syncope
  • Vertigo
  • Blurred vision

Certain drugs can also produce disulfiram-like reactions if alcohol is consumed along with these drugs. Patients should be warned not to use alcohol along with these drugs. The drugs include:

  • Metronidazole
  • Tinidazole
  • Cefoperazone
  • Sulfonylureas

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A patient with chronic kidney disease underwent a nephrectomy. Which of the following can be administered as a postoperative analgesic in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Acetaminophen can be given as an analgesic for the patient as it is the least nephrotoxic among the given options.

Analgesia in CKD patients:

Acetaminophen is considered a safer non-narcotic analgesic in chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients. For more severe pains opioid analgesics like tramadol or fentanyl are used. 

Even though acetaminophen is considered safe, with chronic high dosage it can also become nephrotoxic.

NSAIDs like naproxen, indomethacin, diclofenac, etc are not used in CKD patients because of their direct nephrotoxic effects. In healthy normal individuals, NSAIDs have little effect on renal function and blood pressure. But in conditions where the regulatory systems are impaired as hypovolemia, congestive heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, chronic kidney disease, or other conditions where the renin-angiotensin system is activated, renal function by the formation of prostaglandins are very important.

NSAIDs cause impairment of prostaglandin-induced inhibition of chlorine reabsorption and antidiuretic hormone action. This will cause salt and water retention. It also inhibits COX-2 derived prostaglandins which regulate the renal medullary blood flow and would lead to a rise in blood pressure, increased cardiovascular thrombotic events, and cardiac failure. It can also cause electrolyte abnormalities like hyponatremia and hyperkalemia.
